posts.title: A MacBook win, a surprise hug, and support for my dreams
posts.description: What winning a MacBook through Cardtonic Upskill 4.0 felt like, in a moment that took even me by surprise.
paragraphs: Between one and two in the morning, I was looking at my laptop and praying it would not give up on me. My days start at midnight, and this was another early-hours session of pushing the machine further than it seemed willing to go. In my head, it was wheezing. I still had things I wanted to try.

I am an AI/ML engineer in training. With GenAI assistance, my projects had taken me into retrieval-augmented generation, local-model experiments and trying to tune the behaviour of a Llama-based setup, alongside all the other work I was doing. I called the AI NES. These were learning experiments, not evidence that I had become a production ML engineer overnight.

That night I Googled the best laptops for machine learning and found the model I wanted for the work ahead. My circumstances meant I could not afford it. Hours later, I came across the Cardtonic application on Instagram. The timing was so close to that search, and to that prayer over my struggling laptop, that I experienced it as a little miracle. Not a promise that everything would become easy, but an opportunity I could actually apply for.

Cardtonic's first-review graphic reported 19,275 MacBook-track applications: 10,373 passed that review and 8,902 did not make it through. Those were early screening results, not the final winners. The programme offered 25 MacBooks, separately from its 20 tech scholarships. I eventually became one of the 25 MacBook winners.

Twenty-five winners out of 19,275 applications works out to one winner for every 771 applications, or about 0.13%. That is an overall selection ratio, not a calculation of my personal probability of winning. The scale of it helps explain why I was so excited: being one of those 25 meant a great deal to me.

On Saturday, I broke character. I hugged a business acquaintance in broad daylight because Cardtonic had decided to support my dreams. He looked at me in surprise. I was showing a side of myself he had not seen before, and that was how happy I was. My post on 11 October held that moment: an unguarded reaction, not a carefully composed prize announcement.

I had won a MacBook through Upskill 4.0. The programme describes its prize as an M5 MacBook Pro. That name matters: a MacBook Pro with an M5 chip is not the same thing as an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. I am not assigning my prize an unverified RAM, storage or upgraded-chip configuration.

Apple's specification for the 14-inch MacBook Pro with the base M5 lists a 10-core CPU, a 10-core GPU with Neural Accelerators, a 16-core Neural Engine and 153GB/s of unified memory bandwidth. Shared CPU/GPU memory and that bandwidth make it relevant to running compatible local models and moving model data through the system. That is the published model specification, not a benchmark I have run on my prize.

For my learning, the practical attraction is a machine on which I can develop retrieval pipelines, run suitably sized models locally, and explore parameter-efficient fine-tuning. MLX-LM supports generation, quantized models and LoRA/QLoRA on Apple silicon. The model, context length and training settings still have to fit the actual available memory. The Neural Engine is not a guarantee that every ML library uses it, and a laptop is not a substitute for a cluster training a large foundation model from scratch.

NES has helped me be more precise about what I mean by tuning. Retrieving better context and adjusting a model's prompts do not change its weights. The saved fine-tuning artifacts I can substantiate in the current NES workspace are Qwen3.5-2B QLoRA runs on a separate GPU training path, not proof of a fine-tuned Llama checkpoint or of large-model training on my old laptop. I have written the companion NES post below to explain that work and what it taught me.

The win also helped someone else. My existing laptop went to a university colleague studying computer science who did not own one. It felt like killing two birds with one stone: I could continue my learning on the new machine, and a colleague now had a laptop for their studies. The support did not stop with me.

A stitch in time saves nine came to mind too. I had been hoping my laptop would hold on while I worked out what came next. This opportunity arrived while that need was real, and made it possible to pass on a useful resource rather than simply leave it unused. I cannot put a number on the value of that timing for either of us.

Thank you, Cardtonic, for supporting my dreams and, through this handover, another student's learning too. I am still in training. There is still work to do. But I wanted this first post to keep the feeling intact: a prayer in the early hours, an application appearing on Instagram, a surprised acquaintance, and one very happy hug.

posts.title: NES: my local AI workbench, and the experiments behind it
posts.description: What I am adapting and learning through NES: local-first agents, retrieval, governed tools and Qwen fine-tuning experiments that still have to earn their place.
paragraphs: I called the AI NES. It became the name of the workspace in which I explored a question that mattered to me: how could an assistant help across research, requirements, documents and code without treating every task as a fresh conversation? This is a personal learning project, developed with GenAI assistance, not a claim that I built an entire AI framework from scratch.

My local workspace is a fork that combines existing framework components with personal adaptations. Its README describes a local-first assistant, and the desktop persona is called Ohemaa. Local-first is the intention, not a claim that every feature is always offline: the engine layer can connect to different model providers, and external integrations have their own dependencies and permissions.

The architecture is modular. A conversational interface feeds an orchestrator; the orchestrator can select an agent, a model engine, tools and retrieved context. An Ollama engine adapter is present in the code. The local memory layer exposes storage and retrieval, while traces and evaluation records provide a way to examine what happened. I find this separation useful because a model answering a question, an agent choosing a tool, and a memory store finding a passage are different jobs.

Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is one thread of the work. A query is matched against indexed material, relevant passages are supplied as context, and the model answers with that context available. NES's documented memory options include SQLite full-text retrieval and other backends. Changing the retrieved material or the retrieval settings does not retrain the language model. It changes what information the model sees for that request.

A separate training thread is more concrete than a script labelled fine-tune. Saved run manifests and adapter files identify Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B with LoRA adapters, and the training path uses QLoRA. The records describe a private Kaggle GPU workflow; the inspected run manifest names a Tesla T4. These are separate GPU jobs, not evidence that my old laptop trained the model itself. They are also Qwen artifacts, not a verified fine-tuned Llama checkpoint.

In that experiment, a frozen BM25 retriever supplies five passages, and the adaptation work targets how the model uses evidence, cites it and abstains when an answer is unsupported. Retrieval and weight adaptation are being evaluated together, but they are still different mechanisms. Keeping them separate helps me investigate whether a weak answer came from poor context, poor use of that context, or a training change that did not help.

One result worth keeping in the story is a rejection. The saved v14 candidate completed training and produced an adapter, but its promotion decision was REJECT. Its required correctness improvement did not pass the gate. A completed job, finite training loss or a saved model file was not enough to call it an improvement. I do not present that candidate as a production-ready tuned model.

The control-plane work brings another set of questions into view. The code includes a local-only status and project-inventory API and a Council coordinator. The design separates advisory roles such as architect, critic and operator, and constrains external CLI advisors to read-only advice. The point is not to collect impressive agent names. It is to make capabilities, failures and authority visible before letting a system act.

There are limits that the documentation explicitly keeps open. Cue and Dripwriter are partial sidecar integrations, not proof of a completed screen-to-answer-to-typing workflow. Messaging requires configured, authenticated bridges and approval before sending. The public portfolio assistant is a separate security boundary, not permission to expose private desktop files or memory. A richer provenance-and-supersession memory ledger and clean-machine distribution checks remain hardening work, not completed claims.

That is the learning value of NES for me. I can ask a business-analysis question of my own system: what is the requirement, what has actually been implemented, what evidence proves it works, and what still fails? GenAI helps me explore and build, but it does not remove the need to inspect outputs, protect private information, evaluate changes and say when something is unfinished.

The MacBook opportunity matters in that context. I want more room for compatible local inference, retrieval experiments and carefully scoped adapter work, not a shortcut around the fundamentals. NES remains a workbench for an AI/ML engineer in training. The experiments, including the rejected ones, are part of the education.
